evidence_quotes.quote: This study, through a systematic overview of existing work from Africa, aims to explore critically the role and contribution of LIK systems in water governance and climate adaptation, with the goal of establishing that LIK systems should be understood and operationalised as a water governance system, not as a supplementary knowledge system.

The current research uses a critical thematic literature review as a methodological approach to analyse the conceptualisation and operationalisation of LIK within water governance and climate adaptation policies.

While the review follows systematic principles of transparency and structured selection, it does not use a formal PRISMA methodology because the purpose is interpretive synthesis and conceptual development rather than quantitative meta-analysis.

It draws from evidence from studies conducted in some African countries to analyse the impact of LIK systems on social cohesion, economic gains, and their inclusion in the management of water resources.

In many situations, statutory water legislation coexists with customary water institutions, but formal legislation supersedes customary law. Reforms in water policy should enable the integration of customary allocation laws, management norms, and conflict resolution practices with statutory laws

criterion_notes.c1: Fails Criterion 1 (and matches Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). The paper is a continent-wide thematic and bibliometric review of integrating Local and Indigenous Knowledge (LIK) into broad water resource management and climate change adaptation policy (predominantly rain-fed smallholder agriculture, traditional weather forecasting, flood coping, drought management, and ecosystem stewardship). Aside from brief narrative summaries of a few rural water management case studies within its 30-paper sample, it does not examine household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain wording vs. narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, this paper would pass Criterion 2 in isolation because it examines institutional, legal, and governance factors (legal pluralism, co-management, epistemic hierarchy, and statutory vs. customary water governance). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, Criterion 2 is NO because the review analyses macro-governance, epistemological recognition, and national climate/water-resource policy integration of Local and Indigenous Knowledge rather than a concrete rule-type legal or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility regulation). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because the study fails Criterion 1 and Criterion 4.
criterion_notes.c3: Borderline/unclear for systematic empirical synthesis: the authors searched Scopus, Web of Science, and ScienceDirect (128 records screened to 30 publications) and conducted VOSviewer keyword co-occurrence, thematic coding, and SWOT analysis, but explicitly state that the review does not use a formal PRISMA methodology because its purpose is interpretive synthesis and conceptual development, and 37% of its 30 included items are themselves review papers (6) or book chapters (5), with no new primary data created or analysed.
criterion_notes.c4: Fails Criterion 4. Reported outputs consist of bibliometric keyword co-occurrence counts, document-type counts, SWOT categories, and high-level narrative themes on policy integration of LIK and agricultural/climate resilience. It does not report or synthesize outcomes measuring household or community water or sanitation service access, connection, availability, reliability, continuity, quantity, affordability, or service exclusion.
criterion_notes.c5: Fails Criterion 5 for review scope. While the literature-review procedure (30 publications) is identifiable, there is no defined household/community service-access population, rule-type service-access exposure, or water/sanitation service-access outcome.

study_design: Critical thematic literature review, bibliometric keyword co-occurrence analysis, and SWOT analysis of 30 publications
country: Multi-country (primarily Africa, including South Africa, Zimbabwe, Tanzania, Botswana, Namibia, Cameroon, Ethiopia, Ghana, Malawi, Nigeria, Kenya, and Lesotho, with comparative studies from Australia, Canada, New Zealand, and India)
population_and_sample: 30 publications (19 journal articles, 6 review papers, and 5 book chapters) selected from 128 database records on Local and Indigenous Knowledge in water governance and climate adaptation
exposure: Integration versus marginalisation of Local and Indigenous Knowledge (LIK) systems in formal water resource and climate change adaptation policies
outcome: Bibliometric keyword co-occurrence and document-type distributions, SWOT diagnostic themes, and degree of policy integration of LIK in climate adaptation and water resource management (no water or sanitation service-access outcomes synthesized)
rationale: Excluded under E01 (Wrong topic; see Exclusion Criterion 7, water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). This paper is a critical thematic and bibliometric overview of integrating Local and Indigenous Knowledge (LIK) into broad water resource management and climate change adaptation policies in Africa (focusing heavily on rain-fed agriculture, weather forecasting, flood risk, drought adaptation, and ecosystem management). It neither examines household/community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no) nor reports service-access outcomes (c4 = no), and under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 it addresses macro-governance and epistemic pluralism in resource/climate policy rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (c2 = no). Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, it remains excluded for failing Criteria 1 and 4.
